Weekly Corn and Ethanol Intel Report

Week of August 27, 2026Market data through: August 26, 2026Narrative created: August 28, 2026Nearby corn: $5.103/bu (+$0.315 (+6.6%) week)

Weekly review of corn, ethanol, energy, co-product, policy, and related public-company performance for commodities risk managers at U.S. ethanol plants.

Strategy Narrative

Nearby futures from Yahoo Finance. Nearby corn is the market's current perception of yield and demand risk.

ContractLastWeek changeAs of
Nearby corn$5.103/bu+$0.315 (+6.6%)August 27, 2026
RBOB gasoline$3.384/gal+0.121 (+3.7%)August 27, 2026
Henry Hub$2.907/MMBtu+0.174 (+6.4%)August 27, 2026
  • 1. Crop tour reversed the prior week’s corn-risk improvement
  • 2. Prospective refinery exemptions weakened RIN protection
  • 3. EPA resolved the late-August E15 cliff
  • 4. Exports slowed—but did not reverse—the ethanol stock build

Executive View

  • Field evidence materially challenged USDA’s corn balance sheet. Pro Farmer estimated a 173.2-bushel national yield and 15.344-billion-bushel crop, versus USDA’s controlling August estimates of 180.7 bushels and 16.013 billion bushels. Nearby corn closed at $5.103 per bushel, up $0.315, or 6.6%, for the week, confirming that the market increased—not reduced—the yield-risk premium.
  • Corn procurement is now the dominant plant-margin risk. The 669-million-bushel gap between Pro Farmer and USDA would, if mechanically applied before demand rationing, reduce USDA’s 1.653-billion-bushel projected carryout to roughly 984 million bushels. That is an illustrative sensitivity, not a forecast, but it shows why delayed harvest and first-quarter coverage became more exposed.
  • RFS credit risk deteriorated before any final EPA action. D6 RINs reportedly fell 34 cents to $1.75 on August 24 after EPA signaled an extension of the September 1 compliance deadline and an end-August decision on pending small-refinery exemptions. Administration officials are reportedly considering relief covering 1.2–1.8 billion RINs, but EPA said no decisions had been made.
  • The ethanol balance improved only at the margin. Production rebounded 23,000 barrels per day to 1.112 million, while inventories rose another 85,000 barrels to 25.206 million, 11.8% above last year. Stronger reported exports helped slow the stock build, but output remains high relative to domestic inputs.
  • Energy provided a stronger ethanol price umbrella but higher plant costs. RBOB rose 3.7% and gasoline stocks fell 2.536 million barrels, while Henry Hub rose 6.4%. Midwest gas storage remains 5.9% above its five-year average, limiting scarcity risk but not preventing a near-term cost increase.
  • Overall margin and risk conditions deteriorated: sharply higher corn and natural-gas futures, combined with weaker RIN values, outweighed firmer gasoline and the slower ethanol inventory build.

The incremental thesis is that last week’s weather-based reduction in national yield risk was premature. USDA’s August balance sheet remains the official regime, but crop-tour measurements, deteriorating conditions and a 6.6% corn rally have raised the probability of a meaningful September production cut. Continuing 45Z monetization, regenerative-ag feedstock documentation, monthly ethanol-export strength and carbon infrastructure are not re-narrated because no material new federal or commercial development emerged this week.

1. Crop tour reversed the prior week’s corn-risk improvement

Status: REFUTE

What happened

Pro Farmer’s August 21 national estimate placed corn yield at 173.2 bushels per acre, with a range of 171.5–175.0, and production at 15.344 billion bushels, plus or minus 1%. Scouts reported lower ear populations, shorter grain length and substantial field-to-field variability. USDA’s August 12 survey-based forecast remains 180.7 bushels and 16.013 billion bushels. (Pro Farmer, “Pro Farmer Estimates 2026 U.S. Corn Crop at 15.344 Billion Bushels,” August 21, 2026.) (profarmer.com)

USDA subsequently cut national corn condition by three points to 57% good-to-excellent for the week ended August 23, versus 60% the prior week and 71% last year. The crop was 81% in dough, 41% dented and 6% mature. (USDA NASS, Crop Progress, August 24, 2026.) (nass.usda.gov)

Why it matters

The new field evidence does not prove that USDA is seven-plus bushels too high; crop-tour estimates are not equivalent to USDA’s survey process. However, the magnitude and geographic consistency of the disappointment are too large to dismiss as routine sampling noise. Nearby corn above $5 and up 31.5 cents validates the conclusion that the trade now assigns materially greater probability to tighter supply.

Risk-manager implication

Plants that treated recent rainfall as justification for leaving harvest or winter corn uncovered now face greater futures risk. The first transmission is through December and March corn; local basis will depend on whether tour weakness overlaps each plant’s procurement radius. Directionally: corn bullish, ethanol feedstock cost higher and physical margins lower, with high confidence through the September crop reports.

Watch next

Whether early harvest results validate low ear counts and whether USDA moves yield closer to the Pro Farmer range.

2. Prospective refinery exemptions weakened RIN protection

Status: UPDATE

What happened

EPA plans to extend the current September 1, 2026 deadline for refiners to demonstrate 2025 RFS compliance; a final rule entered White House regulatory review on August 26. EPA also indicated it expected to decide pending small-refinery petitions by the end of August. (Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, “RFS Program: Extension of 2025 Compliance Reporting Deadline,” received August 26, 2026.) (reginfo.gov)

Reuters reported that D6 RINs fell to $1.75 on August 24, their lowest since April 15. Subsequent reporting said administration officials were pressing for exemptions covering approximately 1.2–1.8 billion RINs, versus roughly 1 billion previously contemplated. EPA stated that no petition decisions had been made. (Reuters, “US Ethanol Credit Prices Slump After EPA Delays Biofuel Compliance Deadline,” August 24; “White House Pushes for More Refinery Waivers,” August 26, 2026.) (investing.com)

Why it matters

The immediate impact is on RIN value and obligated-party compliance strategy, not necessarily physical ethanol disappearance. Still, exemptions materially above the assumptions embedded in EPA’s 2026 RVO would weaken the marginal incentive to blend and reduce the value of RIN-linked ethanol contracts.

Risk-manager implication

Treat the reported exemption range as a scenario, not confirmed policy. Plants should separate outright ethanol exposure from D6-linked pricing and avoid assuming the record headline RVO fully protects credit value. The largest near-term exposure is RIN price and counterparty contract value, followed by physical blend demand if EPA does not offset exemptions.

3. EPA resolved the late-August E15 cliff

Status: RESOLVE

What happened

EPA’s August 20 waiver extended the common national gasoline pool containing 9%–15% ethanol through August 31, closing the previously perceived August 29–31 gap. Beginning September 1, EPA permits the earlier transition to higher-volatility winter-grade gasoline through the remainder of the federal summer-control period. (EPA, “National Fuel Waiver to Bring Forward Wintertime Gasoline Beginning September 1, 2026,” August 20, 2026.) (epa.gov)

Why it matters

This resolves the immediate E15 distribution concern identified last week. Once winter-grade gasoline becomes permissible, the summer RVP restriction no longer creates the same E15 constraint. The trade-off is that earlier winter-grade supply can pressure petroleum blending-component values.

Risk-manager implication

The result is supportive for continued E15 availability but not a new structural demand mandate. With RBOB nevertheless rising 3.7% this week, the petroleum price umbrella strengthened despite the additional supply flexibility.

4. Exports slowed—but did not reverse—the ethanol stock build

Status: UPDATE

What happened

EIA ethanol balance Week ended Aug. 14 Week ended Aug. 21 Change
Production, million bpd 1.089 1.112 +0.023
Inventories, million bbl 25.121 25.206 +0.085
Refiner/blender inputs, million bpd 0.926 0.923 -0.003

Inventories remained 11.8% above the comparable 2025 week. The Midwest accounted for most of the weekly build, rising 299,000 barrels to 10.045 million, while East and Gulf Coast stocks declined. (EIA, Weekly Petroleum Status Report, August 26, 2026.) (eia.gov)

Gasoline inventories fell 2.536 million barrels to 206.842 million, with refinery utilization at 97.4%, reinforcing the stronger RBOB environment. (ir.eia.gov)

Why it matters

The stock increase was much smaller than the prior week’s 323,000-barrel build despite higher production, indicating better total disappearance. It does not yet resolve the underlying imbalance: inventories have increased for three consecutive reported weeks and remain historically heavy.

Risk-manager implication

Prompt ethanol exposure improved from “steadily worsening” to heavy but stabilizing. Plants still need export support or maintenance-season production cuts to produce an outright draw. Corn demand remains supported by the 1.112-million-barrel-per-day run rate, intensifying the feedstock squeeze created by the crop-tour estimate.

Strategic Synthesis

The week created a more adverse plant-margin combination: field evidence challenged corn supply just as plants maintained high operating rates, while prospective refinery exemptions reduced regulatory-credit protection. Strong gasoline values and improved ethanol disappearance are meaningful offsets, but neither compensates for a 31.5-cent corn rally unless ethanol prices and basis respond further.

What I’m Watching Next

  • By August 31, 2026: EPA’s targeted decision window for pending small-refinery exemptions and the RFS compliance-deadline extension.
  • August 31, 2026: USDA Crop Progress and Condition.
  • September 2, 2026: EIA ethanol and petroleum balances; REX American Resources fiscal second-quarter results.
  • September 11, 2026: USDA WASDE and Crop Production—the first official opportunity to reconcile crop-tour evidence with the 180.7-bushel yield.

Bottom Line

The most consequential weekly change was the reversal from easing to rising corn-yield risk, confirmed by both the crop tour and a 6.6% nearby-corn rally. Harvest and winter corn coverage now requires the closest attention, while EPA’s end-August refinery-exemption decision is the catalyst most capable of further changing ethanol and RIN economics.

Recent Earnings Highlights — 3m Ret

Companies covered in this section:

  • Deere (DE)

Deere (DE) +19.9%

Reported: August 20, 2026 · Google Finance earnings page

Earnings Call Summary

John Deere delivered strong Q3 2026 results, with net sales and revenues up 5% year-over-year to $12.608B, and equipment operations net sales up 6% to $10.999B. Net income reached $1.379B, or $5.10 per diluted share, comfortably beating the estimated EPS of $4.679. Equipment operations achieved a 14.4% operating margin.

At a Glance

  • Deere Tops Q3 Financial Estimates: Deere & Company reported an adjusted EPS of $5.10, comfortably beating Wall Street expectations of $4.679, while reported revenue reached $10.999 billion to surpass the estimated $10.734 billion.
  • Segment Divergence Drives KPI Resilience: Operating performance was driven by a robust 18% net sales increase in Construction & Forestry and a 12% gain in Small Ag & Turf, which successfully offset a 6% revenue decline in the Production & Precision Ag segment.
  • Full Year Income Outlook Raised: Management narrowed and raised its fiscal 2026 net income guidance to a range of $4.75 billion to $5.00 billion, confidently establishing 2026 as the structural bottom of the current agricultural equipment cycle.
  • Market Responds with Upward Momentum: Following the stronger-than-expected third-quarter results and updated full-year forecast, Deere's shares jumped over 7% during trading on Thursday.
  • Tariff Costs Face Future Headwinds: The company recorded a beneficial $110 million in tariff recoveries during the quarter, but projects a higher net run rate of direct tariff expenses near $1 billion heading into fiscal 2027.

Key Moments from the Call

  • 10m — Fiscal 2026 Guidance Raised on Execution: Deere raised its full-year 2026 net income outlook to $4.75B-$5.00B and equipment cash flows to $5.0B-$5.5B. Strong factory output, disciplined execution, and robust Q4 order books across all segments gave management the confidence to narrow and lift guidance despite dynamic, challenging agricultural end markets.
  • 21m — EOP Signals 2026 as Cycle Bottom: Model year 2027 Early Order Programs (EOP) for planters and sprayers in North America are up mid-single digits year-over-year. Management believes this encourages the view that 2026 represents the bottom of the agricultural equipment cycle, backed by normalized new/used inventory spreads and healthy dealer channel inventory.
  • 25m — Precision Ag Technology Adoption Doubles: Despite a compressed farm economy, technology adoption continues to accelerate. Factory installation trends suggest See & Spray adoption will nearly double, making its way onto 1/3 of North American sprayer orders. Advanced planter technologies like ExactRate and FurrowVision are appearing on over 40% of model year 2027 orders.
  • 33m — Tariff Costs Set to Shift in 2027: Deere lowered its 2026 direct tariff expense expectation to $1.1B (down from $1.2B) due to Section 232 adjustments. However, after factoring in $382M of 2026 refunds that will not recur, net tariff exposure will rise from ~$750M in 2026 to ~$1.0B in 2027, creating a minor headwind.

Company Overviews

Corteva (CTVA)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $52.4B · 3m +3.7% · 12m +10.5% · 24m +49.2%

Google Finance

Largest U.S. corn-seed franchise (Pioneer) and a primary input cost for Corn Belt acres.

Corteva is an agricultural inputs pure play that was formed in 2019 when it was spun off from DowDuPont. The company is a leader in the development of new seed and crop protection products. Seeds generate the majority of profits with the remainder coming from crop protection products. Corteva plans to spin off its seeds business in late 2026. The seeds business will be named Vylor, while the crop protection business will retain the Corteva name and be a pure-play crop protection company following the divestiture. Corteva operates globally, but around half of revenue comes from North America.

Nutrien (NTR)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $33.6B · 3m +7.1% · 12m +26.5% · 24m +52.0%

Google Finance

Largest North American agricultural retailer and a major potash and nitrogen producer.

Created in 2018 as a result of the merger between PotashCorp and Agrium, Nutrien is the world's largest fertilizer producer by capacity. Nutrien produces the three main crop nutrients—nitrogen, potash, and phosphate—although its main focus is potash, where it is the global leader in installed capacity with a roughly 20% market share. The company is also the largest agricultural retailer in North America and Australia, selling fertilizers, crop chemicals, seeds, and services directly to farm customers through its brick-and-mortar stores and online platforms.

CF Industries (CF)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $18.0B · 3m +8.0% · 12m +45.6% · 24m +54.0%

Google Finance

Nitrogen fertilizer producer; corn is the crop that most moves UAN and urea demand.

CF Industries is a leading producer and distributor of nitrogen, which is primarily used in fertilizers. The company operates nitrogen manufacturing plants primarily in North America. CF also produces nitrogen in the United Kingdom and holds a joint venture interest in a nitrogen production facility in Trinidad and Tobago. CF makes nitrogen primarily using low-cost US natural gas as its feedstock, making the company one of the lowest-cost nitrogen producers globally. It is also investing in carbon-free blue and green ammonia, which can be used as an alternative fuel to hydrogen or as a means to transport hydrogen.

Deere (DE)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $156.7B · 3m +19.9% · 12m +28.7% · 24m +68.8%

Google Finance

Dominant North American farm-equipment maker for corn planting, harvest, and grain handling.

Deere is the world's leading manufacturer of agricultural equipment and a major producer of construction machinery. The company is divided into four reporting segments: production & precision agriculture, or PPA, small agriculture & turf, or SAT, construction & forestry, or CF, and financial services, or FS, its captive finance subsidiary. The core PPA business is the largest contributor to sales and profits by far. Geographically, Deere sales are 60% US/Canada, 17% Europe, 14% Latin America, and 9% rest of the world. Deere goes to market through a robust dealer network that includes over 2,000 dealer locations in North America with reach into over 100 countries. John Deere Financial provides retail financing for machinery to its customers and wholesale financing for dealers.

CNH Industrial (CNH)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $16.5B · 3m +10.5% · 12m -3.7% · 24m +14.6%

Google Finance

Case IH and New Holland farm equipment serving corn growers.

CNH Industrial is the world's second largest manufacturer of agricultural machinery (82% of industrial net sales) as well as a major player in construction equipment (18% of industrial net sales).
